title: Believing He Could, So Never Preparing: How the Stunt King Nearly Died in a 4,000-Foot Canyon
dek: Stunt rider Knievel treated "positive attitude" as a methodology: no practice runs, no jump-angle calculations, no risk assessment. Psychology professor Oettingen's experiments show that optimistic fantasy doesn't fuel success — it paralyzes. The Snake River failure was sealed before ignition.
why: This isn't another hero narrative; it puts "think and it will happen" on the lab bench: how positive suggestion made him avoid preparation, how psychology explains it, and how it turned into an accident step by engineering step. The middle section on Napoleon Hill's biography runs long — feel free to fast-forward.
who: Founders, investors, and team leads who often chant "believe first, see later" — anyone who has to pump up morale and make risk decisions at the same time.
skip: If you don't care about the history of success literature, skip 5:28–10:36; the payoff is the psychology experiments and the canyon-jump post-mortem after the 22-minute mark.

points.h: When the countdown began, even he no longer believed
points.body: On September 8, 1974, in front of live cameras, Evel Knievel told a reporter to his face that he wished he weren't there and didn't have to do this. True to form, his method was positive visualization and full throttle — no calculating the ramp angle, no practice runs, no rehearsal. But the Snake River Canyon is roughly 4,000 feet wide, and his previous motorcycle jump record was only 140 feet. As the countdown began, one thought was left in his head: pressing this button might be the last thing he ever did.

points.h: The stunt king's creed was taught to him by an insurance company
points.body: As a young man he made a living selling insurance, once claiming he sold 110 policies in a day, with clients including the staff and patients of a mental hospital; he believed he deserved a vice presidency, and when his boss W. Clement Stone refused him to his face, he quit on the spot. Stone was the co-author of Napoleon Hill's "positive mental attitude" doctrine. The later Knievel lived on this stuff — his later "never prepare, just believe" approach to jumping traces back to this encounter in the insurance business.

points.h: The success guru's biography doesn't survive scrutiny
points.body: Napoleon Hill is treated as the father of modern self-help publishing, wrote Think and Grow Rich, and interviewed Ford and Rockefeller. But the evidence the show presents points to him being a fraud: no record of him serving as an adviser to Wilson; the claim that Carnegie mentored him in writing the book can't be found in the archives; his interview notes "conveniently" disappeared in a fire. Think and Grow Rich was actually his own thousand-page The Law of Success compressed into 230 pages and rewritten as "13 steps to wealth" — yet it sold 100 million copies.

points.h: His first famous jump was improvised mid-air
points.body: After leaving the insurance company, to open up sales for Honda motorcycles, he jumped 40 feet in public without ever having attempted a practice jump; the landing zone was a group of mountain lions and a cage full of rattlesnakes. Mid-air he realized he didn't have enough speed, but improvised by lifting the front wheel — the whole maneuver was written while flying. He landed on the snake cage, man and bike stayed upright, and the snakes instead crawled into the audience — a comical scene. It became the first "victory" of his life, and from then on he was hooked on jumping.

points.h: The more you fantasize about success, the less you clear the obstacles
points.body: NYU psychology professor Gabriella Oettingen's experiments clash head-on with positive thinking: students who fantasized about getting good grades were more likely to fail; patients who fantasized about a smooth recovery from hip surgery stayed in bed longer. Her explanation is that optimistic fantasy lets people "pre-spend" the feeling of achievement, so they don't move to clear the real obstacles; imagining the obstacles is what pulls the trigger on action. The show calls it a counterintuitive conclusion: thinking through the bad outcome first is precisely how you make the good outcome happen.

points.h: Both prototypes sank, and the third carried a person directly
points.body: The engineering for the Snake River Canyon jump was almost never validated: during an unmanned X-1 test flight it spiraled upward and plunged head-first into the Snake River; the modified X-2 prototype also went out of control, coming to rest on the riverbed alongside the X-1. Because of budget shortfalls, engineers are said to have made a valve out of a dog-food can. With only weeks left before the land-lease contract expired, there was no next Skycycle available. So the only option was to put Knievel into the never-flight-tested X-2 for the actual launch.

points.h: His life hung on a single 45-pound grip
points.body: The X-2 was registered as an aircraft by Idaho authorities, and its main controls were just two things: foot pedals controlling the tail fins, and a handle requiring 45 pounds of pressure to hold — hold it and the parachute doesn't open; let go or pass out and the chute fires immediately. He had never flown a plane, never practiced in the cockpit, not even G-force training, and wore only a stars-and-stripes jumpsuit. When asked if he feared passing out mid-flight, he said no, he would stay conscious. The show's narration spells it out: that kind of determination is no substitute for a plan.

points.h: Snake River wasn't one failure — it was the start of the decline
points.body: Everything went out of control the instant of ignition. Knievel felt his "whole field of vision go," perhaps blacking out momentarily; the chute fired early, the craft decelerated violently, and finally grazed the canyon wall and fell into the Snake River, not far from shore, and he lived. Engineer Truax's conclusion: you didn't hold that handle. Knievel blamed the parachute design, and harsher fans said he deliberately popped the chute early and chickened out. Afterward his public performances gradually fell apart — alcoholism, hitting a business partner with a baseball bat, jail — the Snake River jump was the beginning of his long decline.

terms.def: The success philosophy peddled by Hill and Stone: think only good thoughts and misfortune won't find you.
Repeatedly visualizing a wish in your mind and believing it will come true on its own; the show calls Hill's method a forerunner of the manifesting craze.
People who believe good outcomes come only from actively seeking opportunities and doing real work; the opposite of fantasy optimists.
The steam-powered rocket vehicle Knievel had custom-built to jump the Snake River Canyon, registered as an aircraft but never test-flown.
